title: Values, the Stack and the Heap
intro: A Rust variable holds a value itself, not an arrow to an object somewhere else. Where that value lives, on the stack or on the heap, is mostly decided by its type. This lesson explains both places, so every later lesson can use the words.

coming_from.go: A Go struct variable holds its fields directly, and so does Rust's. The difference is who picks the place. Go's escape analysis moves a value to the heap for you when it has to outlive the function; in Rust the type says: a plain value lives in its variable, and `Box`, `Vec` and `String` own heap memory. A `Vec`'s header is the same three words as a Go slice header.
coming_from.kotlin: A Kotlin `class` variable is a reference to an object (normally on the JVM heap), so `val b = a` shares the object. A Rust variable holds the value itself, like a C struct, so `let b = a` copies the value (or moves it), and no second name for one object appears unless you ask for one with `&`, or with `Rc` or `Arc` when several owners need the value.
coming_from.python: In Python every variable is a name for an object, so `b = a` gives one object two names. In Rust a variable holds the value itself. `let b = a` copies the value (for small plain types) or moves it. A second name for the same value is a reference, written `&a`, or an `Rc`/`Arc` when there are several owners; you ask for it.
coming_from.typescript: Objects in JavaScript and TypeScript are always held by reference, so `const b = a` shares the object (`const` fixes the binding, not the object). A Rust variable holds the value itself, so `let b = a` copies it or moves it. To share, you write `&a`, or use `Rc`/`Arc` for several owners.
coming_from.java: A Java object variable is a reference to an object (normally on the heap), so `Point b = a` shares it. A Rust variable holds the value itself, closer to a Java `int` than to a Java `Point`: `let b = a` copies it or moves it, and sharing is something you ask for with `&`, or with `Rc`/`Arc` for several owners.
coming_from.csharp: Rust's variables work like C# `struct` variables: the value sits in the variable, and `var b = a` copies it. There is no `class` kind that shares by default. A reference is a separate thing you write with `&`, and the compiler checks it.
coming_from.c: You already know this: a Rust struct variable is a C struct on the stack, and `Box` is a pointer to heap memory that frees itself. What Rust adds is checking. It knows which variable owns each heap allocation, never frees one twice, and frees it when the owner goes out of scope. It also won't let a reference outlive what it points at.
coming_from.cpp: Same model as yours: locals live in the frame, and `Box<T>` is close to `std::unique_ptr<T>`. Rust adds two things: moves are the default and the old name can't be used afterwards, and the compiler rejects a reference that would outlive its value.

notes: The stack holds function calls' local variables, and is cleaned up when each call returns. The heap holds data whose size isn't known when the program is compiled, or that must outlive the call that made it, among other things.
A `String` or `Vec` is two parts: a small header (a pointer, a length and a capacity) in the variable, and the text or elements on the heap.
Numbers, and a small struct that derives `Copy`, are copied by `let b = a`. Types that own heap memory are moved: the header is copied and the old name stops working.
`size_of::<T>()` tells you how many bytes a type takes in its variable. A `&str` is 16 bytes (a pointer and a length) however long its text is.

python.code:
class Point:
    def __init__(self, x, y):
        self.x = x
        self.y = y

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"({self.x}, {self.y})"


a = Point(1, 2)
b = a  # b is another name for the same object
b.x = 99
print("a =", a)
print("b =", b)

# To get a separate point, you build one.
c = Point(a.x, a.y)
c.x = 7
print("a after c.x = 7:", a)
